B. MEANS OF CONGRESSIONAL INFLUENCE 
OVER AGENCY EXERCISE OF DELEGATED POWER
In this section, we discuss techniques by which Congress has 
influenced agency action short of enacting or amending substantive 
statutes. These techniques have compelled agencies to pay attention to the 
wishes of current Senators and Representatives, even if it has been years 
since any amendment to the legislation that authorizes the agency to act.
1. THE OLD ^LEGISLATIVE VETO”
Starting in the 1930s and up to the 1980s, Congress enacted about 200 
statutes in which it delegated authority to some agency to take some action 
(usually rulemaking, but sometimes adjudication) with the hmitation that, 
if either House of Congress adopted a resolution disapproving the agency 
action within a certain timeframe, the action would be invalid. The 
resolution usually provided by these statutes was a simple resolution, that 
is, only one House needed to adopt it for it to have its effect (of invalidating 
the agency action). Such resolutions were known as “legislative vetoes” 
because one chamber of the legislature was effectively vetoing agency 
action. Occasionally the statutes provided for the agency action to be 
blocked not by a simple resolution but by a concurrent resolution, that is, 
one that required adoption by both the House of Representatives and the 
Senate to be effective (known as the two-House legislative veto). Neither 
type of legislative veto was equivalent to a statute, as neither went through 
presentment to the President as required by Article I, Section 7 (and the 
one-House legislative veto did not even go through the process of 
bicamerahsm required by that Section).
